question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Location and the first printing press established there in colonial India]
options: Goa — First printing press in India established by Jesuits around 1556
Tranquebar — First Tamil printing press established by Ziegenbalg in 1712
Serampore — First Bengali printing press established by William Carey in 1800
Bombay — First printing press in India established by the Portuguese in 1530
wrong_fact: The first printing press in India was NOT established in Bombay in 1530. It was established in Goa by Jesuit missionaries around 1556, making Goa the correct location for India's first printing press.
explanation: The Jesuits brought the first printing press to India at Goa around 1556 (some sources say 1557), making Goa the correct first location. Ziegenbalg set up the first Tamil printing press at Tranquebar in 1712. Carey established the Serampore press around 1800 which produced works in Bengali and many other languages. Bombay had no printing press in 1530 — that is before systematic European presence in the region.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Printing press centre and notable publication/language printed]
options: Serampore — First Bengali translation of the Bible by William Carey (1800)
Tranquebar — First Tamil Bible printed by Ziegenbalg (1714–1727)
Bombay — First Marathi newspaper 'Darpan' printed by Bal Gangadhar Shastri Jambhekar (1832)
Calcutta — 'Samachar Darpan' — first Bengali newspaper printed at Serampore Mission Press (1818)
wrong_fact: 'Samachar Darpan' (1818) was printed at the Serampore Mission Press in Serampore (near Calcutta), not in Calcutta itself. The option incorrectly attributes it to Calcutta while correctly naming Serampore Mission Press.
explanation: William Carey did produce the first Bengali Bible at Serampore around 1800. Ziegenbalg's Tamil New Testament (1714) and full Bible (1727) were printed at Tranquebar. The Marathi newspaper 'Darpan' was indeed founded by Bal Gangadhar Shastri Jambhekar in Bombay in 1832. The error in option 4 is geographic: 'Samachar Darpan' was published from Serampore by the Mission Press — not from Calcutta, though Serampore is adjacent to Calcutta.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Early Indian printing centre and associated vernacular language development]
options: Serampore (Bengal) — Carey's press produced grammars and dictionaries in 40+ Indian languages including Sanskrit, Marathi, Punjabi
Goa — First book printed in India was 'Conclusões e outras Cousas' (1556) in Portuguese/Latin by Jesuit press
Madras — First Telugu printing began with the College of Fort St. George grammars (early 19th century)
Calicut — First Malayalam printing press established by Portuguese Franciscans in 1578
wrong_fact: The first Malayalam printing was NOT at Calicut by Portuguese Franciscans in 1578. The first Malayalam printing press was established at Quilon (Kollam) — and early Malayalam printing is associated with Varthamanappusthakam (1772) by Paremmakkal Thoma Kathanar printed in Rome. Franciscans at Ambalakad (near Calicut) had a press but the date 1578 and location Calicut are both inaccurate.
explanation: Carey's Serampore press was indeed extraordinarily productive across dozens of languages. The first book printed in India was indeed at Goa's Jesuit press around 1556. Fort St. George College in Madras did pioneer Telugu printing and grammar in the early 19th century. The Calicut claim is the error — early Malayalam printing is associated with Quilon and Rome, not Calicut in 1578. The Franciscan Ambalakad press (near Thrissur, not Calicut) was established in 1578 — the location in the option is wrong.
